The lesions look like leaf spot damage to me. It is a fungal disease. You can still eat the leaves (technically), but they don't look very appealing. I get this on my Swiss Chard from time to time. The fungus likes hot, humid conditions, and if your soil stays damp, the conditions are even better for it to grow and spread to your other lettuce plants.

It lives in the soil, so it's really hard to control once you have it. I have used water mixed with a little baking soda and neem oil to keep it from spreading fast (you can find recipes online; try Googling Green and Prosperous with baking soda fungicide), but the best solution is prevention.  Plant your lettuce somewhere else for the next 2-3 years if possible. If that's not possible, you'll have to be diligent about checking the leaves and clipping the diseased ones frequently. Some people also use copper fungicide spray, but I stopped using that years ago and have no idea how well it works for this kind of leaf spot anymore.

I used to hate onion too, and I still hate raw onion.

For any preparation for which you used to put in raw onion, just leave it out. Your burger does not need a wheel of stinky onion. (Or rather, yours can, but his doesn't need it.) If you want to add crunch and flavor, add pickles. If you want to add crunch with less flavor, think about cucumbers or lettuce. Your salad does not need the flavor of raw onion, and if you think it tastes hollow without it, think about what other ways you can bump up the flavor. (Torn-up herbs? Flavored vinegars? More interesting greens to begin with? There are endless possibilities.)

For preparations with cooked onions, where he doesn't like the onion flavor, keep using onions, but just take them all the way. Onions cooked for 30 minutes until they get jammy and soft and brown and thoroughly cooked are not offensive the way raw onions are.

For more specific advice, I'd need to know what you were adding raw or lightly cooked onion to.

It looks like that's being grown inside a wooden box. If it's in a container, that plant has probably taken most of the food out of the soil and is starving. Productive fruiting plants generally deplete soil nutrition fairly quickly in containers. There just isn't enough stored nutrition for them to last long, especially if it's potting soil. 

If that thing is in the ground, it may just be an end of life thing. Last year all of my cucumbers went off the deep end pretty quickly. I'd had plenty of cucumbers so I wasn't too bummed but there was definitely more time in the season for them to yield. 

This year I decided to do a second planting. I just went through with the seed I had left and resowed the row so that if (or when) the more mature plants kick off, the small plants will be there still producing. I have two theories on how it will go, both will be insightful. If the big ones die and the little ones thrive afterwards, then I assume cucumbers have a lifespan. If both of them die about the same time, I'd imagine soil nutrition is to blame.

I just want to proselytize for a moment. I made them for dinner tonight and they were so delicious. I bought them from a great supplier in Maryland but got the frozen ones because I wanted to hold them for a day before cooking them. Honestly, I think they were nearly as good as live!

I usually have them out at restaurants so I had to do a little research. I went with a very simple method of cooking. Dredge in seasoned flour, dip in egg/milk mixture, back into the flour and then into peanut oil to shallow fry. 

I seasoned the flour with cayenne, ground celery seed, onion powder, garlic powder, smoked paprika, salt, msg, and ground mustard  - not a lot of any of those. I also made sure to shake it off thoroughly so the coating was very thin. 

I had considered making a remoulade but didn't bother and I don't think that they needed it. 

If you like them but haven't made them at home, I just want to say that it was fairly easy to do and I rarely fry anything so it is not like I have any skills in that department.

Here's how I make my guac.


I use a Molcajete as a mortar and pestle. I start by grinding several cloves of garlic into a paste with some sea salt.  I add chopped onion and grind that into a fine paste. Then I add tomatoes and grind them into the paste.


After that I add the avocados, one quarter of a fruit at a time, mashing until any big pieces are gone. 


Then I add lime juice and, if needed, additional salt.  Taste testing is important. 


Lastly, I add chopped tomatoes and stir them in for texture. 


I don't add cilantro for two important reasons: some people think it tastes like soap, and my girlfriend prefers guac without the cilantro. 


I have added chopped cilantro on occasion when specifically requested, stirring it on at the end with the chopped tomatoes. 


My Molcajete had made so much guacamole that it turned from light grey rock to a deep, even black from the avocado oil.


Also, I recommend buying a Guac Lock, which will keep your extra guacamole from going brown in the fridge.

AMA was a dishie/line cook/sous chef in 20+ restaurants/pubs/cafes in the UK, now I'm working at a huge fine dining place in Russia. Everything here is different AF.
So in the UK everything is pretty much the same as all the stuff in this sub, some places are understaffed shitholes, with 30+ tickets on at a time 24/7 and it's absolute hell. Some places are extremely well run and organized, and even with tons of massive orders on at a time, everything goes quickly and smoothly. You all know how it is. Also, absolutely everything has to be labeled, dated(date it was made, who made it, and date it needs to be thrown out), and 'use first' stickers stuck onto stuff (e.g new produce was delivered, and there's still old ones. The stickers are so that everyone knows which ones to use first)... And whenever any meat was cooked, the fattest part of it had to be poked with the digital thermometer and it had to be 75degrees C or more. Now matter how busy it is. This was always probably the most strict rule of all. They told us, If any undercooked chicken EVER went out, the place would get shut down, and you'd be fired no second chances. Or even legal issues. The only exception being for beef burgers or steaks, you could tell just by colour how well done it is. I know maybe this is obvious stuff to you guys but I'm just explaining standard procedure for how everything was done in UK, idk if it's the same in the US. Every place I worked at in the UK had the same rules and policies everywhere. Also very strict about preparing raw meat, do it on a red board, far away from other food, then very thoroughly wash your hands and knife before using them to touch anything else (well, I don't have to explain cross contamination lol). And honestly, in the most busy times, like for example after throwing raw chicken into the fryer, you don't have time to go to the sink and wash your hands, but there's like a make-shift container of soapy water (which turns into absolute shit after half an hour) at the chicken/fryer area where you can kinda wash your hands, but you don't have time to dry them with paper towel/blue roll, and just rub them on a dirty tea towel or apron. That's the most 'unhygienic' thing I ever did. Others did it too... Also there was very strict rules about perishable things (meat, pasta, rice, eggs etc.) being at room temp for more than a couple hours. Always had to keep it in the fridge. Ideally, never let anything get to 'bacteria breeding ground' temperature, aka room temperature. All of this is very, very strictly hard-wired into everyone from the moment they start working in a kitchen. Also having to pass fire safety exams and cross contamination exams and training courses every 6 months. Also gloves weren't necessary for anything, but some people chose to use them as heat protection, so they can grab stuff straight off the grill/fryer and without burning your hands too much and work faster that way. But gloves were always optional 



Now, onto how kitchens work in Russia, LITERALLY NONE of what I wrote above applies to them. When I first started working there, I was shocked at everything. Also keep in mind I'm at the most renowned and prestigious place in the whole area. People travel hours to come here. Everyone has weddings/birthdays/big events here, it's like THE place to be. There's even like a mindset that if you ever go out and don't come to THIS restaurant, then you're uncool, uncultured, cheap, etc. Everything is overpriced AF (like over 15$ for a small salad made up of 50grams of potato/cucumber/mayo, like 3 spoonfuls) especially considering russian salaries, $15 is more than what most people earn in a day. But despite this, it's still fully booked every day for months in advance. There's 5 floors, floor 2-5 is for bookings, and floor 1 is for walk-ins. Kitchen is underground, and we send our food on trolleys through a bunch of lift systems. The owner of the place is some billionaire who has 100s of similar restaurants all over Russia. He also owns like 100s of farms, aqua parks, saunas, factories etc. I've talked with this guy a few times and he is pretty cool, but his business model is incomprehensible to me, I mean, all of his buildings are gold plated everywhere inside and outside, all the furniture inside is extremely ornate, (think of like putin's palace or something) I mean one chair is over $50k usd. And there's like 800 of them. In just one building. And not even mentioning the other stuff, sofas, beds, even the god damn TV frame is made of literal gold lol, and all the buildings are made of polished marble. How is he making money from that?! He also has so many of his restaurants/aqua parks in random-ass poverty-stricken shithole towns where no one can afford that stuff and no one ever goes there, but they are fully staffed and running.



Anyway that was off topic, back to how kitchens work here. Shocking thing #1: everyone has their own designated spot, they stay in their place and use their chopping board for everything. This is different cause in the UK it was like white board for bread/cheese, whenever anyone needed to cut up bread or cakes or cheese, they would go to the white board and do it there, yellow board for cooked meat, whenever someone had to cut up something like steak for philly sandwich, they'd go to the yellow board and do it. And blue for fish, brown for veg, green for fruit, but the brown/green ones were treated more like "all other miscellaneous shit" and ofc the red board for raw meat. That thing was treated like the motherfucking plague. Even after being cleaned and through the dishwasher.

 So yeah here everyone uses their one board for everything, cutting raw chicken, and then cutting up fresh veg in a salad ready to eat, without even washing the board or knife or hands 🤦‍♀. The board is the same from the beginning of the shift till the end, it never gets changed or washed. But they occasionally clean it with a spatula type thing which seems to clear up 99.9% of the shit that was on it, even if it was absolutely soaked in raw meat juice/blood, after one scrape with the thing, it looks good as new, and somehow completely dry too. And seemingly it works, since no one has ever got sick or anything. I've even started eating bits and pieces from these boards and then later on remembering 'oh shit they were literally laying on top of raw meat juice and I ate them' and thinking I'm gonna die, but literally nothing happened? I'm even starting to doubt myself, like maybe all those rules about raw meat that were programmed into me from day 1 were all too extreme or something? No one here seems to care. 


Shocking thing #2: the line cooks are mostly women in their 30-40s, the dishwashers are age 70-80 babushkas. The prep cooks are children age 7-12, there is a motherfucking 7 year old girl who cuts and peels onions like an absolute pro. And she can do everything with such precision and speed, just as good as some guy with 10+ years experience. All the little kids are insanely good and doing their jobs. In the UK the whole kitchen team is a bunch of degenerate 20-something males every time. But the bar staff in UK/russia is exactly the same, a bunch of loud ass teenage girls who are constantly talking about getting fucked up every night. And always whinging and whining about everything. 


Shocking thing #3: customers are so nice, polite, respectful, and never ask for weird shit. Less than 0.1% of orders have a request, like "no peppers on the pizza" or "make the fries a little more crispy". But those are totally normal requests and nothing weird. But 99.9% of orders are exactly how it is on the menu. No customers have that "I'm entitled" energy like they do in the west. No one is ever rude or angry if an order was wrong or if they didn't like something. No one demands refunds or does any stupid shit like planting their own hair into it and sending it back. They just say it in a normal way, like "Hey I don't think it's supposed to be like this" and the waitress is like "oh I'm sorry! Thanks for letting me know! I'll go and get it sorted for you right away! once again I'm very sorry!" and everything is sorted without any anger or anything. Also I've noticed that no one ever seems to be in a rush and don't mind waiting. No one ever comes there really 'for a quick bite' and then leave. It's usually for an important event or a date or gatherings. And I don't even think that the food is the main reason they come there, so they don't really care. I mean there's a dancefloor and dj with fog machines and lasers and arcade room and karaoke nights and a bunch of other shit going on lol. Every one of the 5 floors has different shit happening and everyone is free to go anywhere they want, so I think they're more interested in that stuff than the quality or wait time of the food. That's one of my theories anyway. Or maybe people here really are just nicer. 


Shocking thing #4: (this applies to all jobs in all fields in russia btw) whenever there is no orders on, everyone can just sit on their phone or just make themselves something to eat, or chill outside. No manager or boss will shout at you for doing nothing, they also come to sit and chill with us, have a cup of tea and a chat, watch a film, smoke, whatever. This is wildly different to UK work ethics. In the uk if there is ever "nothing to do" you find something to do, "if you got time to lean, you got time to clean"... Yeah they will make you clean all the perfectly clean fridges which have already been deep cleaned 5 times in the past week, they'll make you do it a 6th time. Or some other kind of equally useless task. God forbid you stand around and doing nothing for more than 5 seconds and everyone will start shouting at you for not working. But in russia everyone, including supervisors/managers/bosses understands that it's ok to do nothing sometimes, everything that needs to be done right now is already done, so you can sit around and wait until something else needs to be done. And during moderately slow times, half the cooks can manage, while the othef half sit on their phones, and then they switch after a while. Like hey man you've been on your phone long enough, now it's your turn to cook and my turn to play on my phone lol 


Shocking thing #5: they don't use thermometers to check if meat is cooked, they pierce it with one of those wooden burger skewers and wait 10 seconds, if red or pink liquid comes out, it's not done. If transparent, or brown/white, it's done. Or just cut it to see the colour inside. 


Shocking thing #6: no antibacterial spray for surfaces. No paper towels/blue roll. Just one dirty ass tea towel for the whole day. 


Shocking thing #7: for such a prestigious place, with very high end type of food, and over 1000 things on the menu, I would've thought that work ethics would be different, hygiene would be immaculate, the place of gonna be full of serious, professional chefs. When I first started, I was kinda nervous, thinking this place is gonna be out of my league, but it turned out that their hygiene practices are 10000x worse than anything I've seen, in the UK even a random family pub has better standards.


Shocking thing #8: how disorganized the place is, in terms of getting orders done quickly. If, for example, I get a ceasar salad(one of the most popular orders, dozens are done every day) I would have to go 3 different rooms and 4 different fridges. It takes 5-10 minutes just to collect the necessary ingredients. There can be an order with only 4 things on there and it'll take 4 chefs 30+ minutes to complete. Can't they have the most used things all in one place? And more prep done? So that whenever there's an order they don't spend like 80% of their time finding and chopping up stuff, and it's all done and ready to go straight into the frying pan whenever the order comes. 

Shocking thing #9: they leave staff lunch/food in the heat (30+ degrees, for over 14 hours) pasta, rice, meat, salads, everything... And everyone still eats it 


Shocking thing #10: they are strict about wearing gloves. This is kinda funny cause they think wearing gloves makes them super ultra hygienic and professional. Despite all the other unhygienic stuff they do. And also funny cause this was optional in the UK, and not even a hygiene thing, but a heat protection thing. As long as you wash your hands all the time I don't see the point of gloves, they just get in the way, especially when cutting. 


Shocking thing #11: no one is allowed to carry big pots full of liquid, or sacks of potatoes or crates of meat etc (basically anything heavy) by themselves. You have to call someone to help you. This one is actually pretty sweet, zero chance of doing your back in, or hurting yourself. 


Shocking thing #12: no one is overworked, no one gets angry, no one is stressed, everyone is calm and cool, even during really busy times, everyone just does their thing, listening to music, it's always chill. No one is asked to do too many things at once, tasks get split evenly between everyone. 


#13: you can sit down most of the time, if you're grating cheese, peeling potatoes, stirring onions or whatever, you can do it all while sitting down. And you can even watch videos on your phone while you do it. 


#14: the pizza is absolutely amazing, it's by far the best pizza I've ever had in my life. And it's funny cause the pizza is just like 0.1% of the 1000 things they do. It's so much better than places that literally specialize in just pizza. And genuine Italian places. And the apple strudel is the best dessert I've ever had. And that's really saying something cause I've been to so many nice restaurants in so many countries and tried everything. All their recipes here are actually so good. 



That's all I can think of for now. I just wanted to share this info somewhere. I guess it would be interesting. AMA also if there's any more questions
